intro: Bucaco is a forest behind a wall, and the wall is the reason it exists. Discalced Carmelite friars enclosed this hillside in 1628 and got two popes to protect it in writing, one bull threatening excommunication for anyone who damaged a tree. Four centuries of that produced 105 hectares holding more than 250 species, including the cypress that Philip Miller named after Portugal from specimens he saw here. The six trees on this page stand within about a kilometre of each other, and one of them named a species.
meta_description: Bucaco's ancient trees: the cedar that named a species, Europe's fourth tallest tree, and a bunya pine, all inside one walled forest above Luso.
question_meta: The Cedro de Sao Jose, a Mexican cypress planted between 1628 and 1650 by the Carmelite friars, is the oldest tree in the Bucaco forest.
question_answer: The oldest tree in the Mata Nacional do Bucaco is the Cedro de Sao Jose, a Mexican cypress standing in the forecourt of the Ermida de Sao Jose. The forest's own plaque at its foot says it was planted between 1628 and 1650, which makes it roughly 380 years old and the oldest cedar in the forest. It is not really a cedar, and it is not Portuguese: Cupressus lusitanica comes from Mexico and Central America.
question_context: The friars arrived in 1628 and this tree went into the ground within their first two decades, which makes it one of the first exotic trees planted at Bucaco and probably one of the first of its species in Europe. The species carries the mistake in its name. When Philip Miller described it in 1768 he was looking at specimens growing here, so he called a Mexican cypress lusitanica, after Portugal, and the Portuguese call it cedro-do-bucaco after a forest it never came from. The tree is not what it was. Cyclone Gong tore through Bucaco in January 2013, felled ten notable trees and wrecked around 40 percent of the forest, and it took most of this one's height with it: the register measured 32.9 metres before, and 14 metres after. What stands now is a five and a half metre trunk inside an iron railing, broken at the top, still carrying green. Go expecting a survivor rather than a spire.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Bucaco?
faq.a: The Cedro de Sao Jose, a Mexican cypress planted between 1628 and 1650 by the Carmelite friars. The forest's own plaque calls it the oldest cedar in the Mata. It lost most of its height in the 2013 cyclone and stands as a broken trunk inside an iron railing.

faq.q: Does it cost anything to visit?
faq.a: Walking in is free. Driving in is not: the Fundacao Mata do Bucaco charges per vehicle at the gate, 5 euros for a car of up to five seats and 2 euros for a motorcycle, with no separate parking fee. Leave the car in Luso and walk up and you pay nothing.

faq.q: Can you walk between these trees?
faq.a: Yes. All six stand inside the walled forest within about a kilometre, starting at the Largo do Mosteiro beside the Palace Hotel and ending at the Ermida de Sao Jose. Paths are forest paths and the ground is steep in places.

faq.q: Is the tallest tree in Europe here?
faq.a: No, and it is worth being exact. The Giant Trees Foundation measured the Bucaco mountain ash at 64.90 metres and ranks it fourth tallest in Europe. The tallest is a karri at about 73 metres in the Mata Nacional de Vale de Canas near Coimbra, half an hour away.

trees.name: Wellington's Olive

location.address: Largo do Mosteiro, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: On the night of 27 September 1810 the Duke of Wellington tied his horse to this tree, and the tree is still there while most of the convent is not. Wellington had just fought Massena's French army along the ridge above, in the battle that stopped the third invasion of Portugal, and he quartered himself in the Carmelite convent of Santa Cruz afterwards. Nineteenth century builders demolished most of that convent to raise the Palace Hotel, and the olive survived the demolition by standing in the way: it now sits in the middle of the road across the Largo do Mosteiro, which is exactly where a tree ends up when nobody can quite bring themselves to cut it. It is a modest thing to look at, seven and a half metres tall with a trunk two and a half metres round, and it earns its place on what happened beside it rather than on size. Two centuries of tourists have been shown this tree. The state classified it in 2018 along with the rest of the forest's veterans, and it is the only one of them a general is supposed to have used as a hitching post.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: In the Largo do Mosteiro beside the Palace Hotel, about 2 km uphill from Luso
trees.notes: The register lists an olive at the Largo do Mosteiro, in front of the Fundacao, with no age recorded. Independent sources describe Wellington's tree as an olive standing at the former convent and now in the middle of the road there, which matches this entry's species and position, but no source explicitly links the classified tree to the tradition. Published as a tradition, not as a fact, and the age range is deliberately wide because the register gives none.

trees.name: The Bunya Pine by the Palace Hotel

location.address: Jardim ao lado do Palace Hotel, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: Do not stand under this one in a bad year. The bunya pine makes the heaviest cone of any conifer on earth, up to ten kilograms, roughly a bowling ball, and it drops them from a crown twenty-eight metres up. In its native southeast Queensland the trees fruit heavily every three years or so, and Aboriginal groups travelled hundreds of kilometres for the bunya gatherings that followed, feasting on the nuts inside. Australia now signs and fences these trees in public parks for the obvious reason. This one is five metres round the trunk and has been growing beside the Palace Hotel for about a century and a half, which means it went in while the hotel was still a Carmelite convent and was already substantial when the neo-Manueline palace rose next to it between 1888 and 1905. Araucarias are living fossils, a family that was spread across the southern supercontinent before the continents separated, and the stiff geometric spirals of their leaves look older than everything around them because they are. It is the strangest silhouette in a forest full of imports.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: In the garden beside the Palace Hotel, about 2 km uphill from Luso
trees.notes: Register: 150 years at the 2016 measurement, so about 160 now, girth 5.18 m, height 28 m, crown 14.6 m. Wikipedia's account of the forest names bunya pines among its remarkable specimens, which corroborates species and presence, but the age rests on the register alone. No best_time set: bunya masting is well documented in Australia and not documented for this tree, and inventing a month would be worse than leaving it empty.

trees.name: The Blue Gum on the Hotel Road

location.address: Estrada de acesso ao Palace Hotel, junto ao viveiro florestal, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: Seven metres and fifteen centimetres around the trunk, which is more than any other tree on this page and more than most trees in Portugal. This blue gum sits on the access road to the Palace Hotel near the old forest nursery, forty-five metres tall with a crown thirty-two metres across, and it was classified for what the state politely calls great ornamental and landscape value, meaning somebody looked at it and could not walk past. Eucalyptus globulus is the tree Portugal has an argument about. It arrived from Tasmania in the middle of the nineteenth century, it grows faster than anything native, and it now covers around a quarter of the country's forest area feeding the pulp mills, which is why it is blamed for fires and for draining water tables. That national row makes a specimen like this one easy to overlook. Judge it as an individual instead: a century and a half old, a trunk you cannot get your arms a third of the way around, and bark that peels off in long ribbons to leave a smooth grey and cream column. The leaves smell of eucalyptus oil when you crush a fallen one, and the young growth on a blue gum is a different shape and a different colour from the adult leaves above it.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: On the Palace Hotel access road, about 2 km uphill from Luso
trees.notes: Register: girth 7.15 m, height 45 m, crown 32 m, 140 years at the 2016 measurement, so about 150 now. An independent roundup of Portugal's classified eucalypts gives the same 45 m and about 140 years and places it on the Palace Hotel access road, matching the register position.

trees.name: King Regnans

location.address: Cimo do Vale de Sao Silvestre, na curva da estrada, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: This is the tallest tree in the forest and, on the best measurement anyone has taken, the fourth tallest in Europe. The Giant Trees Foundation put a laser on it and got 64.90 metres, with a trunk eight and a half metres around. The national register, working from an older estimate, says 72.9 metres. That gap is worth stating rather than smoothing over, and the honest version is that it stands somewhere between about 65 and 73 metres, which either way is roughly a twenty-storey building growing out of a Portuguese hillside. It went in around 1880. Eucalyptus regnans is the tallest flowering plant on earth: the record holder, a Tasmanian called Centurion, reaches 100 metres, and nineteenth century Australian foresters claimed felled specimens well beyond that. Portugal is not Tasmania, so a tree of this size here is a century and a half of unusually kind conditions in a sheltered valley. It is also the reason the name King Regnans stuck. Look for it on the bend of the forest road at the head of the valley, and give up trying to photograph the whole of it, because nobody manages that either.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: At the head of the Vale de Sao Silvestre, about 300 m from the Largo do Mosteiro
trees.notes: Height is genuinely disputed: ICNF register 72.9 m and girth 8.65 m at the 2016 measurement; an independent Portuguese roundup gives about 72.6 m and a planting date around 1880; the Giant Trees Foundation, measuring by instrument, gives 64.90 m, girth 8.46 m and an estimated age of 131. The range is published rather than a single figure. Hard rule 8 checked: this is NOT Europe's tallest tree. That is a karri, Eucalyptus diversicolor, at about 73 m in the Mata Nacional de Vale de Canas near Coimbra, measured by the same foundation in 2017. The fourth-in-Europe claim is attributed to the foundation, not asserted by us.

trees.name: The Redwoods of Santo Elias

location.address: Estrada para a Porta da Rainha, diante da Ermida de Santo Elias, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: Two coast redwoods stand in front of a hermitage, about ten metres apart, forty-five metres tall, and roughly eight thousand kilometres from the only place on earth they grow wild. Sequoia sempervirens is native to a strip of fog belt along the coast of northern California and southern Oregon, no more than about fifty kilometres wide, and it is the tallest tree species in the world. The reason it does well at Bucaco is the same reason it does well there: this hillside catches sea mist off the Atlantic, and a redwood drinks through its leaves, taking a substantial share of its water directly out of fog rather than up from the roots. The friars did not plant these. They arrived in the second half of the nineteenth century, when the forest had passed to the state and a fashion for collecting the world's conifers was at its peak, and they are among the earlier redwoods in Europe. Their trunks are about five and a half metres round, wrapped in bark that can grow a foot thick, soft and fibrous, fire resistant, and almost impossible to set alight. The two are near twins and the register separates them only by three centimetres of girth, so stand between them and you have seen both.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: On the road to the Porta da Rainha, about 400 m east of the Largo do Mosteiro
trees.notes: Twins folded: register processos AIP01110429I and AIP01110437I, 10 m apart at 40.37580/-8.36147 and 40.37589/-8.36147, both 45 m tall, girths 5.64 m and 5.67 m, both recorded as standing in front of the Ermida de Santo Elias. One visitor sight, one entry; the second id is recorded in data/leads/bucaco.json. Age of 137 at the 2016 measurement, so about 147 now, rests on the register alone: Wikipedia's account of the forest names sequoias among its remarkable specimens, which corroborates species and presence but not age.

trees.name: The Cedro de Sao Jose

location.address: Adro da Ermida de Sao Jose, Mata Nacional do Bucaco, 3050-261 Luso

trees.story: This tree is the reason a Mexican cypress is named after Portugal. When Philip Miller described the species in 1768 he was working from specimens growing at Bucaco, so he called it Cupressus lusitanica, and the Portuguese returned the compliment by calling it cedro-do-bucaco. Both names are wrong twice over. It is a cypress and not a cedar, and it comes from the mountains of Mexico and Central America, carried back by the Carmelite friars who enclosed this hillside in 1628. The plaque at its foot says it was planted between 1628 and 1650, which makes it about 380 years old and the oldest tree in the forest. It no longer looks the part, and you should know that before you walk down. Cyclone Gong hit Bucaco in January 2013, destroyed roughly 40 percent of the forest and took the top off this one: it stood 32.9 metres before the storm and was measured at 14 metres after. What is left is a trunk five and a half metres round, split and silvered, held inside an ornate iron railing, with green still coming out of the wreckage above. Two popes once threatened excommunication for damaging a tree here. This one took its damage from the weather.
trees.access: Free on foot. Cars pay 5 euros at the forest gate
trees.transport: About 500 m south of the Largo do Mosteiro on the Via Sacra path

trees.notes: Vitality resolved carefully and it nearly went the other way. Publico and RTP write about this tree in the past tense after cyclone Gong of January 2013, and a first read of them suggested it had died. Three things say otherwise: ICNF measured it in 2016 and classified it in 2018, and the 2018 classification statement says none of the classified specimens showed poor vegetative or sanitary condition; a Portuguese species article states it was significantly damaged by Gong but survived and calls it the oldest still existing in the Mata; and a Commons photograph of 17 September 2023 shows green foliage on the broken trunk inside its railing. Flagged rather than clean because the crown is a wreck and a visitor must be told so before travelling. Age comes from the on-site plaque, photographed 2020, which reads: planted between 1628 and 1650, over 350 years, the oldest cedar in the Mata do Bussaco. The register's 372 years at the 2016 measurement, so 382 now, falls inside that range. PHOTO: viewed at full size. It is an honest and dramatic upward shot showing the railing and the surviving green, but it is an extreme low angle and the crown does not read as a tree shape, so it is left at found_needs_check for a human eye on the card crop rather than approved.
